client: Lately, I’ve been feeling completely drained from taking care of my mom. Her Alzheimer’s has been getting worse, and she needs more help every day, but I don’t know how to keep up with it all. I guess I’m not sure if therapy can really change anything—this is just how things are now, right?
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a heavy burden right now, and the exhaustion feels overwhelming. I hear a sense of resignation in your voice—like this is just how life has to be. What would it feel like to imagine that therapy could help you find moments of relief, even if everything else stays the same?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe therapy could help, but it’s hard to imagine relief when everything feels so stuck. I’ve tried so many things in the past, and they either didn’t work or only helped for a little while. I guess part of me is skeptical that anything could truly change this time.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between wanting to believe in the possibility of change and feeling hesitant because of past experiences that didn’t quite meet your hopes. Your tone feels a bit more open than your words suggest—like there’s still a part of you that’s willing to explore this, even if cautiously. What would it look like for therapy to feel different this time, even in small ways?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I am open to trying, but it’s hard to shake the feeling that therapy might just end up being another disappointment. I’ve tried talking to people before, and it felt like they didn’t really get what I was going through. For therapy to feel different this time, I’d need to feel like I’m actually being heard, not just getting generic advice or solutions that don’t fit my situation.
therapist: It sounds like being truly heard and understood is really important to you, and past experiences have left you wary of feeling dismissed or misunderstood. Your openness to trying again, despite that wariness, feels like a meaningful step. What would being heard look like for you in this space—what would help you feel like your unique situation is being recognized?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you acknowledging that—it does feel important to me. But honestly, I’m not sure what being heard would look like here. I’ve tried opening up before, and it feels like people just jump to solutions or assumptions without really getting what I’m going through. It’s hard to trust that this will be different.
therapist: It’s clear that trust is a big part of this for you, and it’s understandable that past experiences have made it hard to feel confident in opening up. Your voice sounds a bit lighter than your words suggest—like there’s a part of you that’s hopeful, even if cautiously so. What would it feel like for us to take this slowly, focusing on understanding before jumping to solutions?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you noticing that—I do feel a bit hopeful, but it’s mixed with a lot of hesitation. Trusting someone feels risky, especially after what I’ve been through. I guess I’m worried that if I open up too much, I’ll end up feeling hurt or misunderstood again. Taking it slow sounds good, but I’m not sure how to even start without feeling vulnerable.
therapist: It makes sense that opening up feels risky—like stepping into unknown territory where you’ve been hurt before. Your hesitation is understandable, and I hear how much you want to protect yourself from feeling misunderstood again. Would it help if we focused on small, manageable steps—like sharing just one thing that feels safe to start with?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess small steps sound okay in theory, but even that feels scary. Every time I've tried opening up before, people either didn't get it or made me feel worse for feeling that way. What if the "safe" thing I share still gets dismissed or judged?
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of small steps brings up real fear—not just about sharing, but about how the other person might respond. Your voice tightens when you talk about past experiences, and I hear how much those moments still sting. Would it help if we named that fear together, rather than trying to push past it right away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
Yeah, naming it might help... but I don't know. It's not just one fear, it's this whole mess of feeling like I'll say something stupid or they'll think I'm weird. Even when people have been nice before, I keep waiting for the moment they'll realize I'm not worth their time. 

I guess what stings the most is when I actually tried opening up before and the person just kind of... changed the subject. Like what I said didn't even matter.
therapist: It sounds like those past experiences of being dismissed or overlooked have left deep marks, and now even the thought of opening up feels tangled with fears of rejection or judgment. Your voice softens when you talk about those moments—like it’s still painful to revisit them. What would it feel like for us to hold space for those fears together, without rushing to fix or change them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
Honestly, the idea of holding space for these fears makes me uncomfortable. I don't want to sit with them—I just want them to go away. It's frustrating because part of me knows I need to face this stuff, but another part is terrified of getting hurt again. 

When you say "without rushing to fix them," that actually makes me anxious. Doesn't therapy exist to fix problems? Why would we just sit with something that hurts so much?
therapist: It sounds like there’s a real tension here—part of you wants relief from these painful feelings, while another part worries that facing them will only make things worse. Your voice drops when you talk about sitting with the hurt, like it feels overwhelming to even consider. What if we could explore this at a pace that feels manageable to you, where "fixing" isn’t the only goal—but neither is staying stuck in the pain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, that makes sense about the tension. I do want to feel better, but sometimes when I try to sit with the pain, it just floods me all at once. Like last week—I tried journaling about why I feel so lonely, and suddenly I was crying for two hours. That’s why I avoid it. What if it just pulls me under completely? 

But the idea of going slower... I guess I’ve never really tried that. I always think I have to fix everything at once or not at all. Do you really think that would help without making things worse?
therapist: It sounds like that journaling experience left you feeling overwhelmed—like opening the door even a little let in more than you could handle at once. Your voice speeds up when you talk about it, like you're reliving that flood of emotion. What if we thought of "slower" not as avoiding the pain, but as learning how to let it in without it sweeping you away—like turning a faucet instead of opening a floodgate?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about the faucet metaphor, but it still feels scary to even turn that knob a little. Last time I tried journaling, all these memories and regrets came rushing out, and I couldn't sleep for days afterward. I worry that any amount of opening up will just lead to that same overwhelming flood again.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd feel cautious after such an intense experience—that flood of memories and regrets sounds truly exhausting. I hear how much you want to protect yourself from being overwhelmed again, even as part of you recognizes that shutting everything out isn't working either. What would it look like to experiment with opening up just a tiny bit—maybe with something that feels less charged than those big memories?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
